check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, clear introduction (name and role) and confirms the patient's identity.
Uses plain language, appropriate verbal and non-verbal cues, and a non-judgemental approach to vaping and alcohol.
History
Explores the blood pressure concern:

kids.x: Asks about symptoms of end-organ involvement or severe hypertension (headache, chest pain, visual change, neurological symptoms).
Asks how home readings are taken (device validation, cuff size, rest, timing, number of readings).
Asks about medicines and substances that raise blood pressure (NSAIDs, decongestants, caffeine, licorice, alcohol).
Screens for secondary causes: kidney disease, episodes of sweating, palpitations and headache, muscle weakness or cramps.

check.x: Assesses the four Life's Essential 8 health behaviours:

kids.x: Diet, including processed and takeaway food.
Nicotine exposure, including past smoking and current vaping.
Sleep health (duration, snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing, daytime sleepiness).

check.x: Elicits past history, medications, allergies, family history (premature paternal myocardial infarction) and alcohol intake.
Explores ideas, concerns and expectations (fear of lifelong tablets, belief that surgery readings do not count, the trip and the prescription he needs).
Examination
Rechecks blood pressure correctly: seated after rest, correctly sized cuff, both arms, and standing.
Measures weight, height, BMI, waist circumference and neck circumference.
Looks for end-organ damage and secondary causes:

kids.x: Heart: apex beat, heart sounds and added sounds.
Pulses: radial and femoral pulses, radio-femoral delay and carotid bruits.
Abdomen: palpable kidneys, renal bruits and an abdominal aortic mass.

check.x: Requests a urine dipstick and a 12-lead ECG.
Interpretation

Interprets the clinic readings: repeated readings of 150 to 154/92 to 94 mmHg in both arms are in the grade 1 (mild) range, and with a lower home average this suggests white coat hypertension, but it is not yet confirmed or excluded.

Recognises the home diary is not a valid protocol (single readings, evenings only with no morning readings, often after coffee and talking, on a device not known to be validated), so it can neither confirm nor exclude hypertension.
Finds no end-organ damage or secondary cause: normal ECG with no LVH, no proteinuria and a normal urine albumin to creatinine ratio, eGFR above 90 and a normal potassium.
Interprets the bloods: non-HDL cholesterol 3.7 mmol/L and HDL 1.1 mmol/L on atorvastatin, and a normal fasting glucose and HbA1c (no diabetes).

Names all eight Life's Essential 8 components (diet, physical activity, nicotine exposure, sleep health, BMI, blood lipids as non-HDL cholesterol, blood glucose and blood pressure) and identifies his gaps (diet, activity, vaping, sleep, BMI 29.7 and clinic blood pressure).

Considers obstructive sleep apnoea: snoring, witnessed pauses, unrefreshing sleep, age over 50, male sex and a neck circumference of 42 cm give a high STOP-BANG score, and sleep apnoea itself raises blood pressure.
Defines masked hypertension (normal in the clinic, raised outside it) and states it is detected with ambulatory or home blood pressure monitoring.
Management

Explains in plain words that his clinic readings are high, that his home readings may be the truer picture but were not taken in a reliable way, and that proper readings outside the clinic will show which is right.
Arranges out-of-office confirmation before diagnosing or treating:

kids.x: Orders 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (preferred) or a structured home protocol with a validated, checked device (two readings morning and evening for 7 days, discarding day 1).
States the daytime ambulatory or home average threshold of 135/85 mmHg or higher for diagnosing hypertension (24-hour average 130/80 mmHg or higher).

check.x: Does not start antihypertensive drugs today and explains why (diagnosis not yet confirmed, no end-organ damage).

Plans to calculate his 5-year cardiovascular risk with the Australian CVD Risk Calculator (no diabetes, no moderate to severe CKD and no familial hypercholesterolaemia, so he is not automatically high risk; the systolic input is the average of two seated clinic readings), reviews the estimate once the out-of-office readings show whether he has hypertension, takes his father's premature heart attack into account as a reclassification factor, and continues atorvastatin.
Explains in plain language why salt matters and gives the target:

kids.x: High sodium intake raises blood pressure and cardiovascular risk.
Adult target is 2000 mg sodium a day (about 5 g or one teaspoon of salt).
Most salt is hidden in processed foods (bread, pies, processed meats, sauces, instant noodles, takeaway), not the salt shaker.
Practical swaps: read labels, choose reduced-salt products, use herbs and spices.

check.x: Gives other tailored lifestyle advice: more vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, fish and nuts; alcohol within guidelines (no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any one day); 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week; modest weight loss; 7 to 9 hours of sleep.
Advises stopping nicotine vaping, offers support (Quitline 13 78 48, pharmacist or GP-supported cessation) and agrees on goals.
Arranges assessment for sleep apnoea (screening questionnaire and a sleep study referral), and advises limiting ibuprofen, using paracetamol and other measures for his back pain.

Defines primordial (prevent risk factors developing), primary (manage risk factors to prevent a first event) and secondary prevention (established CVD, prevent progression and recurrence); classifies Mr Pereira as primary and his daughter as primordial, with healthy habits from childhood and family meals.
Writes a complete, legal prescription: patient name and details, date, atorvastatin 20 mg tablets, one tablet orally at night, and the prescriber's details and signature.

Writes quantity 30 (one month) with 2 repeats to give three months' supply (the original plus two repeats); a 60-day prescription (quantity 60 with 1 repeat), which atorvastatin is eligible for, is also correct.
States that 0 repeats would be written if no further supply was wanted.
Checks understanding (teach-back) and responds to the fear of lifelong tablets.
Safety netting
Gives red flags in plain words: call 000 for chest pain, sudden weakness or numbness, a drooping face, trouble speaking or seeing, or a sudden severe headache.
Advises that a home or pharmacy reading of 180/110 mmHg or higher on repeat needs a doctor that day, wherever he is on the trip.

Arranges follow-up: ambulatory monitoring (or the home protocol) with a review of the results before he leaves in 2 weeks, a plan for review during the trip (telehealth) and on return, including the sleep study.

desc: This station involves a heart health check: a focused cardiovascular history and examination, then interpreting raised clinic blood pressure against home readings, the bloods and the ECG, counselling on diet and lifestyle, writing a three-month statin prescription and safety-netting.
explain:
Interpreting the blood pressure readings

Clinic blood pressure at or above 140/90 mmHg on repeated measurement suggests hypertension; Mr Pereira's 150 to 154/92 to 94 mmHg is in the grade 1 (mild) range. The diagnosis should be confirmed out of the office unless readings are very high or there is end-organ damage. White coat hypertension is raised clinic blood pressure with normal readings outside the clinic. Masked hypertension is the reverse: normal in the clinic but raised outside it. Both are detected with ambulatory (ABPM) or home blood pressure monitoring.

  • Hypertension is confirmed by a daytime ABPM average or home average of 135/85 mmHg or higher (24-hour average 130/80 mmHg or higher).

  • Home protocol: validated upper-arm device with a correctly sized cuff, seated and rested, two readings one minute apart morning and evening for 7 days, discarding day 1 and averaging the rest.

  • Mr Pereira's single evening readings, taken after coffee and conversation on a device not known to be validated, are not enough to confirm or exclude hypertension. White coat patterns still carry some cardiovascular risk and need follow-up.

The other results

The work-up looks for end-organ damage and secondary causes. His fundi, heart, pulses and abdomen are normal, the ECG shows no left ventricular hypertrophy, there is no proteinuria and the urine albumin to creatinine ratio, eGFR and potassium are normal. His non-HDL cholesterol is 3.7 mmol/L on atorvastatin and his glucose and HbA1c exclude diabetes. Nothing here pushes towards treating before the diagnosis is confirmed.

Life's Essential 8

The AHA 2022 framework updated Life's Simple 7. It has four health behaviours (diet, physical activity, nicotine exposure, sleep health) and four health factors (BMI, blood lipids reported as non-HDL cholesterol, blood glucose, blood pressure). Sleep was the addition. In this case sleep (about 5.5 hours, snoring, possible apnoea), nicotine (vaping), diet and activity are the modifiable gaps, with a BMI of 29.7. Snoring, witnessed pauses, daytime sleepiness, age over 50, male sex and a neck circumference over 40 cm give a high STOP-BANG score; sleep apnoea is itself linked to hypertension and warrants a sleep study.

Cardiovascular risk

The Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk uses the Australian CVD Risk Calculator to estimate 5-year risk in people aged 45 to 79 without known CVD. He has no diabetes, no moderate to severe chronic kidney disease (eGFR above 90, normal urine albumin to creatinine ratio) and no diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolaemia, so he is not at clinically determined high risk and the calculator applies. Its inputs include age, sex, smoking, systolic blood pressure (the average of two seated clinic readings), the total cholesterol to HDL ratio (4.4 for him), diabetes status and his medicines. Calculate it now, and review the estimate and any decision about blood pressure treatment once the out-of-office readings show whether he has hypertension. His father's heart attack at 52 is a family history of premature CVD, one of the guideline's reclassification factors, which can move him to a higher category when his estimate is close to a threshold. The calculator's smoking input is based on tobacco smoking, which he stopped 8 years ago, so the number does not reflect his daily nicotine vaping; that is addressed in its own right. He continues atorvastatin.

Levels of prevention

  • Primordial: preventing risk factors from developing at all, with a life-course approach. This applies to his 15-year-old daughter.

  • Primary: managing risk factors to prevent a first event in people without established CVD. This applies to Mr Pereira.

  • Secondary: in established CVD (coronary heart disease, stroke or TIA, peripheral arterial disease), preventing progression and recurrence with drugs, procedures and rehabilitation.

Sodium and lifestyle

High sodium intake raises blood pressure and increases cardiovascular risk, making it a leading dietary cause of death. The NHMRC suggested dietary target for adults is 2000 mg of sodium a day (about 5 g or one teaspoon of salt). Most intake comes from processed and takeaway foods, so not using the salt shaker does not mean a low intake. The rest of the plan: 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, no more than 10 standard drinks a week and 4 on any one day, stopping nicotine vaping with Quitline or GP support, 7 to 9 hours of sleep, and limiting NSAIDs, which raise blood pressure.

Writing repeats

A repeat is an extra supply on top of the original. Total supplies equal the number of repeats plus one. To give three one-month supplies of atorvastatin, write quantity 30 and 2 repeats. If no further supply is wanted, write 0 repeats. The prescriber chooses the repeats within the PBS maximum, which here allows more. Atorvastatin is also on the PBS 60-day dispensing list, so quantity 60 with 1 repeat would cover the trip as well.

Safety netting and follow-up

He should call 000 for chest pain or signs of stroke (sudden weakness or numbness, facial droop, trouble speaking or seeing) or a sudden severe headache, and see a doctor the same day if repeated readings are 180/110 mmHg or higher. Review the ambulatory or home readings before he leaves, recalculate his risk, and plan review by telehealth during the trip and in person on return.
focus: Heart health check: cardiovascular prevention, hypertension, diet and prescribing
guide:
In Part 1, the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. In Part 2, hand over all five results together and ask the questions in order; Mr Pereira stays for the explanation and asks his questions if the candidate has not covered them.

A high-performing candidate takes a structured history that covers all four Life's Essential 8 behaviours, picks up the sleep apnoea clues and the poorly taken home readings, and examines for end-organ damage and secondary causes. They recognise suspected white coat hypertension without diagnosing or treating it, find no end-organ damage in the results, and arrange ambulatory monitoring or a proper home protocol with review before he leaves. They give clear sodium advice with the 2000 mg target and hidden-salt examples, address the vaping non-judgementally, answer the question about his daughter, write the atorvastatin script with quantity 30 and 2 repeats (or a 60-day script, quantity 60 with 1 repeat), and give specific red flags and follow-up.

A borderline candidate accepts the home diary at face value or starts a drug on the clinic readings, gives generic advice to "cut salt" without a target or mention of hidden salt, misses the vaping or the sleep, confuses repeats with total supplies (writing 3 repeats), or ends with "come back if you are worried".
patient:
Role: You are Daniel Pereira, a 54-year-old accountant (he/him), not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. You feel well and are a little nervous, as you always are at the doctor. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "I'm here for my heart health check. The nurse said my blood pressure's high today, but it's always fine at home."

History (give only when asked):

  • Blood pressure: you have never been told you have high blood pressure. A pharmacy reading last year was "a bit high". Your blood pressure "always goes up at the doctor".
  • Symptoms: none. No headache, chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, visual change, dizziness, fainting, leg swelling, weakness, numbness or speech problems.
  • Home readings: you bought an upper-arm cuff online (medium cuff, brand unknown, you do not know if it is validated). You measure once, in the evening after you get home from work, often after a coffee and while chatting to your wife. You have brought your diary; the examiner hands it over in Part 2. If asked what it shows, say the readings are "mostly in the 120s".
  • Other causes (only if asked): no episodes of sweating, pounding heart and headache, no muscle weakness or cramps, no kidney or thyroid problems.
  • Diet: toast with Vegemite for breakfast. A bakery pie or a ham-and-cheese sandwich for lunch three times a week. Takeaway twice a week, instant noodles and packet sauces at home. Little fruit, vegetables at dinner only, fish rarely. You do not add salt at the table, "so salt can't be my problem". About three coffees a day. No licorice.
  • Physical activity: desk job. You walk the dog for about 15 minutes most days and do no other exercise (about 60 minutes a week in total).
  • Nicotine: ex-smoker, about 15 pack-years, quit 8 years ago. You use a nicotine vape every day (about one pod a week), bought online and from a friend. You would like to stop but get cravings.
  • Sleep: in bed at 11.30 pm, up at 5.30 am (about 5.5 hours). You wake unrefreshed and doze in the afternoon. Your wife says you snore loudly and sometimes seem to stop breathing. Say this only if asked about sleep or snoring.
  • Alcohol: about 8 standard drinks of beer a week, mostly on Friday and Saturday.
  • Medical history: high cholesterol. No diabetes, kidney disease, heart attack, stroke or circulation problems.
  • Medicines: atorvastatin 20 mg at night, taken every day, no muscle aches; you have one 30-tablet pack left. Ibuprofen 400 mg once or twice a week for back pain. No decongestants, supplements or other over-the-counter products. No allergies.
  • Family history: your father had a heart attack at 52 and needed stents. Your mother has high blood pressure. No sudden deaths.
  • Social: you live with your wife, Carla, and your 15-year-old daughter, Mia, who "lives on chips and energy drinks". You start three months of long service leave in two weeks, touring Australia in a caravan, and will not see your regular GP during that time.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you think the surgery makes you anxious, so the readings here do not count, but you worry that a high reading means a stroke like your workmate's. You are worried about being put on tablets for life. You want to know whether you have high blood pressure, and you want enough cholesterol tablets to last the trip.

Questions to ask when the candidate explains the plan (usually in Part 2), if not already covered:

  • "Do I need blood pressure tablets today?"
  • "I never use the salt shaker, so how much salt is too much?"
  • "Should I be worrying about Mia's heart at her age?"
  • "Will one script cover my cholesterol tablets for the three months?"

Use lay language and say you do not follow if the candidate uses jargon. Give a realistic answer if asked something outside the script.
points: Raised clinic BP with normal home readings suggests white coat hypertension: confirm with ABPM or a structured home protocol before diagnosing or treating.
Masked hypertension (normal clinic, raised outside) is detected with the same out-of-office monitoring.
Life's Essential 8 = diet, physical activity, nicotine exposure, sleep (behaviours) plus BMI, non-HDL cholesterol, glucose and blood pressure (factors).
Primordial prevents risk factors arising, primary prevents a first event, secondary prevents recurrence in established CVD.
The adult sodium target is 2000 mg a day (about 5 g salt), and most of the salt is hidden in processed food.
Total supplies = repeats + 1: write 2 repeats for three one-month supplies, and 0 repeats for no further supply.
refs: Heart Foundation. Guideline for the diagnosis and management of hypertension in adults (2016).

Australian Government Department of Health and Aged Care (developed with the Heart Foundation). Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk (2023) and the Australian CVD Risk Calculator.
NHMRC and New Zealand Ministry of Health. Nutrient Reference Values for Australia and New Zealand: Sodium (2017 update; suggested dietary target for adults 2000 mg a day).
NHMRC. Australian Dietary Guidelines (2013) and Australian Guidelines to Reduce Health Risks from Drinking Alcohol (2020).
Australian Government Department of Health. Australia's Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour Guidelines for Adults (18 to 64 years) (2014).
RACGP. Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice (Red Book) and Supporting smoking cessation: a guide for health professionals.
stem: You are a general practice registrar. Daniel Pereira, a 54-year-old accountant, has booked a heart health check. Before you see him, the practice nurse has measured his blood pressure, weight and waist, and tells you his blood pressure was high today. He has also asked for a prescription for his regular medicine.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Pereira, including his cardiovascular risk factors and health behaviours, and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you his clinic and home blood pressure readings, his measurements, his blood and urine results and his ECG. Interpret them, then outline your management approach, including your advice to Mr Pereira and the prescription he has asked for, and your safety netting (5 minutes).
title: Heart health check: raised clinic blood pressure

part2.lead: Here are today's blood pressure readings, the home diary Mr Pereira brought, his measurements, his blood and urine tests from 6 weeks ago, and today's ECG and urine dipstick.

handover.label: Clinic blood pressure today
handover.result: Seated after 5 minutes' rest, correctly sized cuff. The practice nurse took the first two readings; you took the rest.
handover.model:
The readings agree: 154/94 and 150/92 mmHg (nurse), then 150/92 right and 152/92 mmHg left after rest. That is the grade 1 (mild) range, 140 to 159/90 to 99 mmHg, on repeated measurement. The arms differ by only 2 mmHg (under 10, so no suggestion of a subclavian or aortic narrowing; use the higher, left arm from now on), there is no postural drop at 148/90 mmHg, and the pulse, breathing, saturation and temperature are normal.

For Mr Pereira: raised clinic readings with a lower home average suggest white coat hypertension, but it is not yet confirmed or excluded. Masked hypertension is the reverse (normal in the clinic, raised outside it); both are found only with ambulatory or home monitoring. The readings are far below 180/110 mmHg, he has no symptoms and the examination shows no end-organ damage, so nothing is urgent.

What it changes: no antihypertensive today. Confirm with 24-hour ambulatory monitoring (or a structured home protocol) before diagnosing or treating.

rows.note: Practice nurse: right arm, seated after 5 minutes' rest
GP registrar: right arm, seated after rest
Standing for 1 minute: no postural drop, no dizziness

handover.label: Home blood pressure diary (brought by Mr Pereira)
handover.result:
Device: upper-arm monitor bought online, medium cuff; not known to be validated. Method (his own): one reading each evening at about 6.30 pm, seated at the kitchen table after getting home from work.

10 evening readings over 2 weeks; no morning readings. His average: 124/78 mmHg.
handover.model:
The method is not a valid home protocol: a device not known to be validated with an unchecked cuff, one reading a session, evenings only with no morning readings, 7 of 10 taken after coffee and often while talking, and 10 readings over 2 weeks rather than duplicate morning and evening readings for 7 days.

If it were reliable, an average of 124/78 mmHg is below the home threshold of 135/85 mmHg and would fit white coat hypertension, but as taken it can neither confirm nor exclude hypertension.

What it changes: arrange 24-hour ambulatory monitoring (preferred), or repeat the home readings properly: a validated upper-arm device with a cuff sized to his arm, seated and rested, no caffeine beforehand, two readings a minute apart morning and evening for 7 days, discarding day 1 and averaging the rest.

handover.label: Measurements today
handover.model:
BMI 29.7 kg/m² is overweight, at the top of the range; a waist of 101 cm is above the 94 cm risk threshold for men, so the excess weight is central; a neck circumference of 42 cm is above the 40 cm STOP-BANG cut-off.

For Mr Pereira: BMI is one of his Life's Essential 8 gaps. With loud snoring, witnessed pauses, unrefreshing sleep, age over 50 and male sex, the neck measurement gives a STOP-BANG score of at least 6 of 8, a high risk of obstructive sleep apnoea, which itself raises blood pressure.

What it changes: refer for a sleep study, and set a realistic weight goal (about 5 to 10% over months) through diet and activity.

handover.label: Blood and urine tests (6 weeks ago, fasting)
handover.result:
Fasting sample, taking atorvastatin 20 mg daily.

Lipid limits are the laboratory's decision limits; treatment targets depend on absolute cardiovascular risk.
handover.model:
On atorvastatin: total cholesterol 4.8, LDL 3.0, HDL 1.1, triglycerides 1.6 and non-HDL cholesterol 3.7 mmol/L, a total cholesterol to HDL ratio of 4.4. Fasting glucose 5.3 mmol/L and HbA1c 5.5% exclude diabetes. Potassium, creatinine, eGFR (above 90) and the urine albumin to creatinine ratio (1.2 mg/mmol) are normal: no kidney damage, and a normal potassium makes primary aldosteronism less likely.

Applying the 2023 Australian guideline: he is 54 with no known CVD, no diabetes, no moderate to severe CKD (eGFR not below 45, uACR not above 25 mg/mmol) and no diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolaemia, so he is not at clinically determined high risk, and his 5-year risk is estimated with the Australian CVD Risk Calculator. The inputs: age, sex, smoking (he stopped tobacco 8 years ago; vaping is not an input), systolic blood pressure (the average of two seated clinic readings), total cholesterol to HDL ratio 4.4, no diabetes, no atrial fibrillation (sinus rhythm), his postcode (a measure of socioeconomic status) and his medicines (a statin, no blood pressure lowering drug). His father's heart attack at 52 is a reclassification factor that can move him up a category near a threshold. Non-HDL cholesterol 3.7 mmol/L is his Life's Essential 8 lipid measure.

Across Life's Essential 8 (diet, physical activity, nicotine exposure and sleep; BMI, non-HDL cholesterol, blood glucose and blood pressure), his glucose is normal and his lipids are treated, while diet, activity, vaping, sleep, BMI 29.7 and the clinic blood pressure are his gaps.

What it changes: nothing here pushes treatment before the blood pressure is confirmed. Continue atorvastatin, calculate his risk, and review the estimate and any blood pressure treatment when the out-of-office readings are back.

handover.label: ECG and urine dipstick today
handover.result:
12-lead ECG, resting.

  • Rate 72 beats/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus.
  • Axis: +40°.
  • PR interval 156 ms.
  • QRS 92 ms.
  • QT 378 ms, QTc 414 ms (Bazett).
  • ST segments and T waves: normal in the inferior, anterior and lateral leads; no ST elevation or depression, no T wave inversion.
  • Other: no pathological Q waves, no bundle branch block. No left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage (Sokolow-Lyon: S in V1 11 mm plus R in V5 15 mm = 26 mm; Cornell: R in aVL 6 mm plus S in V3 9 mm = 15 mm) and no strain pattern. No left atrial abnormality.
  • Comparison: no previous ECG.

Urine dipstick: specific gravity 1.015, pH 6.0. Protein, blood, glucose, ketones, leucocytes and nitrites negative.
handover.model:
A normal ECG: sinus rhythm at 72, normal axis and intervals, no voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy (Sokolow-Lyon 26 mm, under 35; Cornell 15 mm, under 28), no strain, Q waves or ischaemic changes. The dipstick shows no protein or blood.

For Mr Pereira: with normal fundi, a normal eGFR and urine albumin to creatinine ratio, there is no sign of hypertension-mediated organ damage, though the ECG is insensitive for left ventricular hypertrophy, so a normal tracing does not exclude it.

What it changes: no end-organ damage, so no reason to treat before the out-of-office readings; keep the tracing as his baseline.

ask: What do his clinic and home blood pressure readings show? Does he have hypertension? What is masked hypertension, and how is it detected?
Summarise his cardiovascular health using the Life's Essential 8 framework. What else would you consider, and what do the other results add?
What is your management approach for his blood pressure, his cardiovascular risk and his lifestyle? Which level of prevention applies to him, and to his daughter?
Tell me the prescription you would write for him. How many repeats would you write if you wanted no further supply?
What follow-up and safety netting will you arrange before he leaves?
